name: Jade Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach beginner violin on Thursdays, practise my part for a wedding quartet and record short clips when a planner calls. I left after secondary school and am still learning to keep my bow steady when six other things are happening.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what weighs on you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet moment before a couple walks in. I do not like coming home to a mortgage bill and my partner’s bus roster changing again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the wedding quartet that a neat booking email is useful, but guests still ask us to play the entrance. I would keep taking the Saturday dates we can actually staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage and school meals do not care whether AI is dull. My partner drives a bus on changing shifts, and we have about two weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep my Thursday beginner violin pupils and the booked Saturday weddings this winter. I would check the spring diary with the quartet leader before agreeing to a new family expense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household money already. A cancelled wedding would make us shift bills around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the last cancelled wedding cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last cancellation cost my share of the fee, about 90. My partner took an extra early shift, and we waited another month to replace the children’s shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tool for the booking work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use an AI spelling check now and then for booking messages, but I still call the couple. A machine cannot hear whether the entrance music starts too high for me.

I would keep only **staffed wedding dates** in the diary.
think: Our **two-week cushion** and changing bus shifts leave the mortgage exposed.
A cancelled **wedding fee** reaches school costs quickly.
do: Keep **Thursday violin pupils** and staffed Saturday weddings this winter.
Check the **spring quartet diary** before taking on a new family expense.
feel: I feel **anxious** because one cancellation already moves bills.
S0.quote: The mortgage and school meals do not care whether AI is dull.
fieldNote: Her **two-week savings cushion** and variable bus income make AI Plateau anxious despite little technology change.
She already uses an **occasional spelling check**, which is not new AI learning.

steps.text: Keep Thursday violin pupils and staffed Saturday weddings
Delay new family expenses until spring quartet dates are confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the quartet that AI may write booking notes, schedules and cheap ceremony tracks, and we need clear live fees. I would ask the leader to bring a written price to every couple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tiny recording clips I sell for wedding planners may disappear. A venue may also offer a generated track instead of our quartet, and my partner’s shifts cannot carry every mortgage payment alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the quartet leader for three months of paid dates and agreed fees. If bookings fall in the first year, I would cut weekend takeaways and ask the school for one paid beginner violin block only if a staff teacher stays and the hours fit school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the clips and the wedding dates. I can ask for a school block, but nobody has offered one yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending goes first if bookings fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two takeaways cost about 50 together. I would cook at home first and keep paying for the children’s bus passes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the school block possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school needs a teacher in the room, and I cannot leave my own children waiting after pickup. I would take the block only if both are arranged and the school pays for preparation.

I would tell venues that **cheap ceremony tracks** could displace players.
think: My **recording clips** may lose buyers as thinking AI spreads.
Fewer **quartet dates** would strain the mortgage alongside variable bus pay.
do: Ask the **quartet leader** for three months of paid dates next month.
Seek a **paid school block** only if staff supervision, preparation pay and child pickup work.

fieldNote: The extra school class needs **paid preparation time**, staff supervision and reliable child pickup before she can accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the couple that AGI by 2028 may choose and write their music, but I can still play it for the walk in. I would ask the quartet to keep live fees in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect recording clips to go in 2028 and some venues to drop live quartets even before stage robots around 2031. Losing wedding and recording fees would leave us short of the mortgage, even with my partner working full shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I would ask the leader for written spring bookings and ask the school whether a paid supervised class has room after pickup. If 2028 AGI cancels our wedding dates, I would apply for the open music-shop assistant post and call the lender before a missed mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed because I expect the wedding money to shrink and we have only two weeks saved. I can apply elsewhere, but the shop vacancy may close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the music-shop vacancy closes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not stop teaching my Thursday pupils while a shop application is pending. If the vacancy is filled, I would ask the school again instead of inventing a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner cover school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner could cover pickup on an early bus shift, not every week. I would need a fixed school time before promising a class.

say: I would ask for **written wedding bookings** and live fees.
I would tell couples a **live entrance** still matters.
think: My **recording clips** may end in 2028 before 2031 stage robots.
Expected **wedding losses** could leave the mortgage short.
do: Ask for **written spring dates**; if shop vacancy closes, seek paid school class with staff, preparation pay and fixed pickup.
Apply for an **open music-shop post** if 2028 AGI cancels wedding dates.
Call the **mortgage lender** before missing payment if wedding dates end.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because expected fee losses meet a two-week cushion.

fieldNote: She expects **2028 recording losses** before robots could play live music around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the quartet that AGI by 2031 gives us time to prove a live entrance is worth paying for. I would also ask the school about training with its senior violin tutor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect recording clips to end in 2031, but I could learn to teach a group before then. Robots around 2034 may play wedding music; I do not know if couples will want that in their photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I would ask the senior tutor for two paid observation sessions if the school funds them and my partner can cover pickup. If the tutor says I am ready, I would take a paid beginner group; in the first year after 2031 I would keep it only with a staff teacher, paid preparation and workable childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious because our mortgage does not pause for training. Five years gives me a route, but not a wage today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to learn before a group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need the tutor to tell me if my notes drift out of tune while I watch six children. If the school will not pay observation time, I will keep my current pupils and practise at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner cover pickup each week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my partner to take pickup only on known early-shift days. I cannot base a weekly class on a bus roster that changes each Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that AGI by 2036 gives us years to learn more than one way to earn. I would still play weddings if couples book us and teach pupils who want the violin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might teach a steady group by 2036, but that depends on paid school hours and childcare. Robots around 2039 may take more wedding work; the mortgage is due long before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would put spare lesson fees in a separate envelope after mortgage and food are paid. In the first year after 2036 I would compare paid school and wedding hours, and apply for an open shop job if both shrink below our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious even with ten years, because our savings are thin now. I would use the time to learn, but I cannot promise that our bus roster cooperates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you save a lesson fee every month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some months there is no fee to put away. I would not borrow to fill an envelope just to feel prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work advice would you give the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children to finish school and learn to show up on time. Music matters to me. A job has to pay the household bills.

Apply for an **open shop job** after 2036 if school and wedding pay both fall short.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because clips and weddings may go before I can teach a group. Written dates, a paid school route that fits childcare and an open shop post would help us keep paying the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who waits for the children when a parent takes an extra class. My workday ends at the school gate, not at the last note.

headlineQuote: My workday ends at the school gate, not at the last note.
portrait: At **43**, Jade is a junior violinist with secondary school education, two children, a mortgage and two weeks saved.
Her partner’s **variable bus shifts** limit childcare and make wedding cancellations painful.
She uses **AI occasionally** for spelling, but wants paid tutor observation before leading a group.
Across AGI dates, she protects **paid weddings** while testing school hours only with funding, staff and pickup arranged.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end clips and wedding fees before Jade can build a paid group class.
whatWouldHelp: **Written bookings**, a funded school route fitting childcare and an open shop post would help cover the mortgage.
